Reb Yisrael Yosef shuffled through the doorway of the shul with his head bowed and his shoulders hunched.

There, on the bed inside, was Reb Yisrael Yosef’s longtime teacher,

Rav Mordechai Yoffe, who was the author of the halachic work called “the Levush”. Rav Mordechai was shivering slightly under his thick woolen blanket, yet at the same time, beads of sweat formed like tiny raindrops around his temples. A bowl of soup, cold and untouched, lay on a wooden table beside him.

Reb Yisrael Yosef squeezed his eyes shut. Perhaps it was because—for a moment, at least—he wanted to forget the

sight of his beloved rebbi in this state. There had been many meetings with his rebbi in better times. First, there was the day when, as a young bachur, he’d passed the test to enter Rav Mordechai’s yeshiva. Since then, he’d been to this room hundreds, if not thousands, of times. Rav Mordechai had been there to clarify his questions in learning, answer his sha’alos in halacha, and guide him in his personal life.

Reb Yisrael Yosef breathed in deeply, opened his eyes, and took a step towards Rav Mordechai’s bed. There were two other men in the room, too; also long-time students. Rav Mordechai had called them together. He wished to give over his parting words

Reb Yisrael Yosef sat down on a wooden three-legged stool. Rav Mordechai laid trembling, bony fingers on Reb Yisrael Yosef’s head.

thing that you’ve been sorely lacking. Take my advice, Yisrael Yosef: begin to study kabbalah. And then … when you have a son … promise that when your son is

twenty years old, you will send him to a recognized mekubal to learn kabbalah as well.”

Reb Yisrael Yosef skipped a breath. Did his rebbi say… a child?

“Promise, Yisrael Yosef.” Rav Mordechai now pressed his palms firmly onto Reb Yisrael Yosef’s head. His voice got a little louder. “Promise you will send your son to

Reb Yisrael Yosef hesitated for a moment. “The Rav knows … I’m a plain Yid, content with learning Gemara and halacha. I was never one to dabble in sifrei kabbalah.”

word, and I’ll give you mine. A bracha that by this time next year, you’ll have a son.”

Reb Yisrael pictured his wife, his father, and his mother, all overjoyed at the news. He pictured himself, for the first time, holding a child in his arms. Rav Mordechai had tried to convince him to learn kabbalah many times over the years, and he’d always declined. But this was an offer he couldn’t refuse. “Yes, Rebbi. I promise.”

A warm smile spread across Rav Mordechai’s face as he removed his hands. “May the Eibershter bentch you with a son. A son who will be illuminated with Torah, and become a luminary for the entire Jewish people.”

Just a few days later, on Gimmel Adar Sheini, Rav Mordechai passed away. Reb Yisrael Yosef soon moved from Posen and settled in Zamoshtch. He began to learn kabbalah regularly, fulfilling his promise to his teacher. It was in his new home, a little under a year later, that his wife gave birth to a baby boy. They named him Yoel.

learned kabbalah, he didn’t expose young Yoel to it right away. He first wanted his son to master Gemara and halacha, and learn kabbalah only later, when he would be more mature.

soon knew too much for the teachers in the local cheder, and Reb Yisrael Yosef had to hire tutors to teach him privately. At age fifteen, Yoel became the youngest talmid in the elite yeshiva at the time: the yeshiva of Rav Yoel Sirkis in Brisk.

Almost everyone, that is—except for Reb Yisrael Yosef. Finally, after much tossing and turning, Reb Yisrael Yosef decided to get out of

bed. Perhaps learning a little or walking around a bit would tire him out enough to go to sleep.

He had just finished celebrating the sheva brachos of his beloved son, Yoel. And Yoel’s twentieth birthday would be next week. In other words, it was time to fulfill the other half of the promise which he’d made to his teacher all those years ago: It was time for Yoel to study kabbalah with an expert.

An expert. But who? Reb Yisrael Yosef wondered, pacing the wood floor. He himself was certainly

no expert. But who would Rav Mordechai want him to choose? Reb Yisrael Yosef wanted to make sure he was fulfilling the promise in full. He therefore decided to start fasting every Monday and Thursday, and daven that Hashem give him the wisdom to know what to do.
